Chlamydia trachomatis is the bacterium responsible for the sexually transmitted infection chlamydia. Similarly, Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, another sexually transmitted infection. Molecular testing methods, such as those targeting DNA or RNA, are often used to detect these pathogens, as opposed to immunologic tests that identify antigens or antibodies. In certain enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) for HIV antibody detection, a higher optical density (indicating more intense color) generally correlates with a greater presence of antibodies. However, these tests are designed to provide qualitative results, such as reactive or non-reactive. Biological specimens are often collected at one site and transported to another for testing and storage. Specimen tracking forms, whether paper-based or electronic, are used to document the journey of specimens from collection through processing, testing, shipping, storage, and eventual disposal. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) and test kit instructions provide guidance on optimal specimen handling and storage. Specimens should be stored in clearly labeled refrigerators or freezers (e.g., Refrigerator No. 2 or Freezer No. 3) to facilitate easy retrieval. Documentation should include the initials or identification of individuals handling the specimens at each step, along with any additional locally determined information. An example of a specimen tracking form is provided in Appendix I-13. When specimens are transported to off-site or referral laboratories, a transport form accompanies them. This form includes details such as the name of the person (e.g., driver) receiving the specimens, the date and time of pickup, the temperature of cool boxes (if used), and the date and time of delivery to the laboratory or storage site. Appendix I-14 provides an example of a specimen transport driver log. Temperature logs should be maintained for refrigerators, freezers, and transport containers. Monitoring should be performed at the start of each workday using calibrated and certified laboratory thermometers. For transport containers, thermometers that record minimum and maximum temperatures during the holding period are recommended. Appendix I-16 provides examples of specimen temperature monitoring logs. Test results are recorded on a designated form, similar to how survey questionnaires capture responses. These results may be entered into a separate database from the survey interview data. The two datasets can later be merged using participant identification numbers to link biomarker test results with interview data. Appendix I-17 provides an example of a test results log. The target population for a survey is the group of individuals about whom researchers aim to draw conclusions. This population is often broadly defined, such as men who have sex with men (MSM) in Mexico City, but may include individuals who are not eligible to participate, such as those who are not sexually active or too young to provide informed consent. The survey population is a subset of the target population, narrowed down based on practical considerations like sampling methodology and eligibility criteria. Eligibility criteria for participation in a survey are typically based on factors such as age, recent risk behaviors, sex, and location of work or residence. For example, a survey of female sex workers (FSWs) may define eligibility as being 15 years or older and having exchanged sex for money or goods at a brothel within the past six months. For MSM, eligibility may include men aged 15 years or older who have had anal sex with other men in the past six months. For people who inject drugs (PWID), eligibility may require being 15 years or older and having injected drugs within the past 30 days or six months. Eligibility criteria should be precise, time-bound, measurable, and reliable. Screening for eligibility involves asking potential participants a series of questions to determine if they meet the survey's criteria. For example, PWID may be asked to show track marks or describe the injection process, while MSM or FSW may be probed about their knowledge of venues or terminology associated with their behaviors. Exclusion criteria may also apply, such as intoxication or prior participation in the survey. Sampling is the process of selecting individuals from a source population to participate in a survey. This allows researchers to gather information about the population without studying every individual, reducing time and cost. Sampling strategies determine how the sample is selected and whether statistical inferences can be made about the source population. An appropriate sampling strategy generates unbiased estimates that accurately describe the population, can be compared with other populations, and are consistent with estimates from other surveys or time points. Sampling bias occurs when some members of the population are systematically more or less likely to be included in the sample, leading to biased estimates. There are two types of sampling error: systematic and nonsystematic. Nonsystematic (random) sampling error results from taking a sample rather than measuring the entire population and can be reduced by increasing the sample size. Systematic sampling error, caused by poor sampling design or protocol violations, cannot be predicted or accounted for. Nonprobability sampling methods, such as convenience, quota, and snowball sampling, are often used for hidden or hard-to-reach populations but produce estimates of unknown precision and reliability. Stratified sampling involves dividing the population into homogeneous subgroups before sampling to reduce variability and improve precision. Cluster sampling is used when it is impractical to list all individuals in the population but possible to list locations or clusters where they gather. For example, sampling at venues or sites where the target population congregates can make the process more manageable and cost-effective.
